domains.title: Hwanin, Lord of Heaven
domains.subtitle: the supreme source of the Dangun founding myth
domains.lead: Hwanin is the supreme celestial figure who rules from heaven in the Dangun founding myth in Korean tradition. The name means "Lord of Heaven" and belongs to the domain "Supreme God, Heaven." In the Samguk Yusa, Hwanin is the ruler of heaven who answers the Buddha's request for a land fit for his teachings by sending his son Hwanung to earth. Hwanin is not a creator in the biblical sense; he is the apex of a celestial hierarchy that authorises the descent of culture and law to the Korean peninsula.

cards.name: Lord of Heaven
cards.desc: Hwanin sits at the apex of the Korean celestial order, the source from which legitimate authority descends.

cards.name: Celestial Court
cards.desc: Heaven is imagined as a court with ministers, retainers, and an ethical law that mirrors human government.

cards.name: Ancestor of Hwanung
cards.desc: Hwanin authorises the descent that makes possible the birth of Dangun and the founding of Korea.

cards.name: Moral Order
cards.desc: The myth encodes the belief that rulers and peoples are accountable to a higher heavenly standard.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Hwanin is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

myths.title: The Request from Heaven
myths.text: According to Iryeon's Samguk Yusa, the Buddha asked Hwanin whether there was a land on earth where his teachings could flourish. Hwanin looked down and saw the Korean peninsula, then offered his son Hwanung to descend with heavenly attendants and sacred regalia.

myths.title: The Descent of Hwanung
myths.text: Hwanin granted Hwanung three heavenly seals and three thousand retainers. Hwanung descended beneath a sandalwood tree on a high mountain, bringing laws, grains, and the arts of civilisation to the human world.

myths.title: Hananim and Korean Religion
myths.text: The vernacular title Hananim became the standard Korean Christian name for God, while in folk and shamanic contexts Hwanin remains the celestial ancestor of the Korean people. The two usages live in parallel, one theological and one mythological.

etymology.derivation: The name is composed of the Sino-Korean elements 桓 (hwan, "spreading, majestic") and 因 (in, "cause, origin"). Read 환인 in Korean, it denotes the supreme celestial authority in the Dangun myth cycle.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Hwanin, the Hangul form is 환인 and the Hanja form is 桓因. Hangul ‘환인’ and Hanja ‘桓因’, the forms used in the Samguk Yusa; the name is also rendered ‘Hananim’ (하나님) in Korean vernacular usage. The ASCII form hananim is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Hwanin is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Hwanin entered Korean Christian vocabulary as Hananim, the name for the biblical God, while in shamanic and nationalist discourse he remains the mythic ancestor of the Korean people. The two traditions interpret the name differently—one as a personal deity, the other as a celestial title—but both preserve the sense that Korea's legitimacy flows from heaven. Confucian and Buddhist interpreters have also read Hwanin through their own categories, sometimes as a personification of cosmic principle and sometimes as a devotional figure.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hwanin survives in Korean public life chiefly through the Dangun myth, which is taught in schools, celebrated on National Foundation Day (Gaecheonjeol), and invoked in discussions of Korean identity. The name Hananim remains one of the most common words for God in Korean Christianity, while Hwanin continues to appear in scholarly reconstructions of early Korean religion, in museum exhibitions on Gojoseon, and in cultural diplomacy that presents Korea as a nation with ancient, heaven-blessed foundations.
lore.extendedMeditation: Hwanin invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition: it marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names.
